messages.content: I need to design live firmware updates for an embedded controller. The update has to preserve real-time deadlines and actuator consistency even when the state schema changes. How should I frame the goal?

Frame it as two obligations that must hold together. During an uninterrupted update, control must continue to meet its 1 ms deadlines, and actuator commands must be neither duplicated nor skipped. Separately, an incompatible state migration must be rejected atomically, and after any reset during an update, recovery must produce a compatible firmware-state pair. A design that satisfies only the timing obligation or only the state-compatibility obligation would not meet the goal.
Does meeting the 1 ms requirement mean the update can pause control briefly and make up the time afterward?

No. The requirement is to maintain the 1 ms control deadlines throughout an uninterrupted update. Catching up later would not undo a missed deadline. The point is continuity while the update is taking place, not merely acceptable average timing over the whole update.
And the actuator condition is separate from the timing condition?

Yes. Meeting every 1 ms deadline would not, by itself, establish that the actuator command sequence is correct. The design must also avoid issuing a command twice or omitting a command during the uninterrupted update. Conversely, an intact command sequence would not excuse a missed control deadline.
Should I read that as requiring exactly one actuator command every millisecond?

Not from the stated goal alone. It specifies 1 ms control deadlines and prohibits duplicated or skipped actuator commands; it does not define a one-command-per-millisecond rule. The design needs to preserve the intended command sequence while meeting the control deadlines, without assuming a command rate that has not been specified.
What changes when the firmware update also changes the state schema?

The state must remain meaningful to the firmware that uses it. A schema change raises the question of whether the existing state can be migrated into a form compatible with the updated firmware. The goal does not specify particular fields or a migration procedure; it does require that an incompatible migration be rejected atomically rather than leaving a partly changed state to be used.
What exactly does “atomically” add to rejection?

It means rejection must not leave a partial migration as the effective result. An incompatible migration cannot be treated as rejected while some of its state changes remain in effect and others do not. This is a consistency requirement, not a specification of a particular storage or update mechanism.
Does that tell us which schema changes count as compatible?

No. Compatibility has to be assessed, but the goal does not define a compatibility rule or enumerate acceptable schema changes. What it does say is how the design must behave when a migration is incompatible: reject it atomically. It also requires a compatible firmware-state pair after an update-time reset.
Why phrase recovery as a firmware-state pair instead of just saying the firmware must recover?

Because recovering firmware alone would not establish that it can correctly use the recovered state. The post-reset outcome must be compatible as a pair: the firmware and the state it will operate on must agree. The requirement does not say that recovery must always select the most recently introduced firmware or a particular schema version.
Does “after any update-time reset” include a reset while the state migration is in progress?

Yes. “Any update-time reset” makes the recovery obligation independent of where the reset interrupts the update, including during a state-schema transition. The required outcome is a compatible firmware-state pair. That statement does not prescribe the internal recovery steps or which compatible pair is selected.
Would it be fair to say a reset must not expose a half-migrated state to firmware that cannot interpret it?

Yes, that captures the compatibility concern. After an update-time reset, recovery must produce a firmware-state pair that is compatible, rather than leaving firmware to operate on an incompatible partial state. Keep that distinct from specifying a particular way to detect, store, or repair such a state; none is given here.
I want to be careful about the word “uninterrupted.” Do the 1 ms deadlines and the no-duplicate-or-skip condition also claim control continues through a reset?

The stated continuous-operation condition applies throughout uninterrupted updates. A reset is addressed by a separate requirement: recover a compatible firmware-state pair after any update-time reset. It would overstate the goal to claim, solely from this wording, that control deadlines continue to be met through the reset itself.
Could a design meet the recovery requirement if the firmware and state each look valid on their own?

Not necessarily. The requirement concerns their compatibility with each other, not just whether each component can be read or loaded independently. Recovery needs to leave a pair in which the firmware can use the accompanying state consistently.
So the acceptance criteria should keep timing, actuator commands, migration rejection, and reset recovery distinct?

Yes. For an uninterrupted update, ask whether every 1 ms control deadline is maintained and whether actuator commands are issued without duplication or omission. For a state-schema change, ask whether an incompatible migration is rejected as a whole. For any reset during the update, ask whether the recovered firmware and state are compatible. Keeping those questions distinct helps avoid treating success on one as proof of the others.
Can you put the design target in one sentence without committing to an implementation?

Design live firmware updates that meet every 1 ms control deadline and neither duplicate nor skip actuator commands during uninterrupted operation, atomically reject incompatible state migrations, and recover a compatible firmware-state pair after any update-time reset.

I have a proposed structure for the live update: run an immutable 1-ms control island with sequence-gated actuator writes, and atomically commit validated firmware-state pairs via dual-slot descriptors. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the design goal. The immutable 1-ms control island is the proposed way to keep time-critical control running while an update proceeds. Sequence-gated actuator writes address command consistency at the actuator boundary. The dual-slot descriptors are the proposed means of committing a validated firmware-state pair as one coherent choice, including when the state schema changes. All three have to work together; the proposal alone is not yet proof that the deadlines and consistency requirements hold.
What does “immutable” mean here? Does it mean firmware can never change?

In this proposal, it means the 1-ms control island is not itself changed as part of the live update it is sustaining. That gives the time-critical path a stable basis while other firmware and state are being updated. It does not, by itself, make a claim about whether or how the control island might ever be changed in a different operation.
So is the island a separate processor?

The proposal does not specify that. “Control island” identifies a time-critical part of the design that remains immutable during the update; it does not prescribe a processor count or a physical partition. Whatever form it takes, its intended role is to keep the 1-ms control work from being interrupted by the live update.
Does calling it a 1-ms island already establish that every deadline is met?

No. The name expresses its intended timing role, but the design would still need to show that the island can meet each 1 ms control deadline throughout an uninterrupted update. In particular, work associated with preparing or committing the new firmware-state pair must not prevent that time-critical work from meeting its deadline.
How does sequence gating relate to the actuator commands?

The proposal puts a sequence check at actuator writes, so a write can be assessed in relation to the intended command sequence. That is a way to guard against duplicate or out-of-order writes during an update transition. It must also preserve the other half of the requirement: legitimate actuator commands cannot be skipped. Merely blocking repeats would not establish that the full command sequence reaches the actuator.
Could the gate simply ignore any command whose sequence looks unexpected?

That would need care. Ignoring a duplicate is different from silently losing a command that was supposed to be issued. The proposed gate has to be understood against both constraints—no duplicated commands and no skipped commands—while control continues to meet its 1 ms deadlines. The proposal does not specify the exact sequence policy or how an unexpected sequence is resolved.
Is the sequence gate intended to replace the control island?

No. They serve different purposes. The immutable control island is aimed at continuous, deadline-bound control during the update. Sequence-gated writes are aimed at actuator-command consistency. A correctly timed control cycle could still produce a duplicate or omission at the actuator boundary, and a correctly gated write would not make a late control cycle timely.
What is being committed by the dual-slot descriptors: the firmware, the state, or both?

The proposal is to commit a validated firmware-state pair. The important unit of commitment is the pairing, rather than an independently chosen firmware version and an independently chosen state. The descriptors are the proposed way to make that paired choice atomic; the statement does not specify the underlying storage layout of either firmware or state.
Why use two descriptor slots?

Two slots are part of the proposed commit structure: they provide places to represent a candidate pair and a committed choice without treating a partially prepared change as a completed switch. For the proposal to meet the goal, the effective selection must change atomically to a validated pair. The exact descriptor fields, write ordering, and atomic operation are not specified here.
Is it accurate to say the new firmware can become effective first and its migrated state can catch up afterward?

That would not express this proposal. It calls for atomic commitment of a validated firmware-state pair, so the effective choice is the compatible combination, not a firmware change followed by a separate effective state change. Preparation may be discussed separately from commitment, but the proposal does not set out a preparation procedure.
What does “validated” require us to establish?

At minimum, the pair being committed must be suitable to treat as a compatible firmware-state pair; that matters especially across a state-schema change. “Validated” is a condition on the proposed commit, not a claim that a particular validation method has already been chosen or carried out. The proposal does not define a schema-compatibility test or list validation checks.
If a state migration is incompatible, would the descriptor still switch so the system can report the problem?

No effective switch to that incompatible pair would fit the stated goal or this proposal. An incompatible migration must be rejected atomically, while the proposed descriptor commit is for validated pairs. How the incompatibility is reported is not specified; it should not require treating an incompatible pair as committed.
Does atomic rejection mean no migration work can begin until compatibility is known?

Not necessarily. Atomic rejection concerns the effective result: an incompatible migration must not leave a partial migration in effect. The proposal does not say whether or how a candidate state is prepared before validation. What matters for the proposed commit is that an incompatible candidate is not made the effective firmware-state pair.
How would the dual-slot idea matter if a reset occurs in the middle of the update?

The intended role is to make the committed choice recoverable as a pair, even if a reset interrupts update work. After any update-time reset, recovery must produce a compatible firmware-state pair; it must not combine firmware selected from one candidate with state from an incompatible one. The proposal identifies dual-slot descriptors as the commit structure, but does not specify the reset-recovery selection procedure.
Would recovery always pick the newest pair?

That is not stated. The recovery requirement is compatibility of the firmware-state pair after any update-time reset, not selection of the newest candidate. A candidate that has not been validated and atomically committed cannot be assumed to be the effective pair just because update work on it began.
I want to avoid suggesting that two descriptor slots mean two complete copies of everything.

That distinction is worth keeping. The proposal explicitly says “dual-slot descriptors,” not “two complete firmware-and-state copies.” You can describe the descriptors as supporting atomic selection of a validated pair without asserting how many full firmware images or state copies the design stores.
Does the descriptor commit itself have to fit inside one 1 ms control interval?

The proposal does not give a duration for the commit. Its timing obligation is that control continues to meet its 1 ms deadlines throughout an uninterrupted update, including when commit activity occurs. Thus, whatever the commit entails, it cannot cause a control deadline to be missed; that does not imply a stated commit-time limit of 1 ms.
Could there still be an actuator glitch right when the effective firmware-state pair changes?

That is precisely a boundary the design must handle. Atomic commitment protects the coherence of the firmware-state choice, while sequence-gated actuator writes are proposed to preserve the command sequence at the actuator boundary. Neither phrase alone proves that the transition has no duplicated or skipped command, so the interaction between them would need to satisfy that requirement.
Would it be misleading to describe this as a completed solution?

Yes. It is a design proposal: keep a 1-ms control island immutable during live updates, gate actuator writes by sequence, and atomically commit only validated firmware-state pairs through dual-slot descriptors. Whether a concrete implementation actually maintains every 1 ms deadline, avoids duplicate and skipped commands, rejects incompatible migrations atomically, and recovers a compatible pair after any update-time reset remains to be established.
How can dual-slot commits recover a compatible firmware-state pair if power fails between migration validation and descriptor activation?

The key distinction is between a candidate that has passed validation and a pair that has become the committed choice. If power fails before descriptor activation, recovery should not infer that validation alone made the candidate active. In a dual-slot design that preserves the previously committed firmware-state pair, recovery can select that pair while treating the unactivated candidate as incomplete update work. That depends on the previous pair still being intact and on recovery being able to distinguish a committed descriptor from an uncommitted one.
So validation and activation are not the same event?

Right. Validation answers whether a proposed firmware-state pairing is suitable to commit. Activation changes which pairing is effective. The power-failure interval in your question exists precisely because the first may have happened while the second has not. Treating a validation result as though it were an activated descriptor would erase that distinction.
If the migration was already validated, why not just finish activating its descriptor after power returns?

That might be possible only if recovery can establish that the candidate firmware, candidate state, and evidence needed to trust their validation are still intact and correspond to one another. The question does not establish those conditions. Selecting the previously committed compatible pair is the conservative interpretation of a failure before activation; resuming or completing the candidate would need its own justified recovery rules, not an assumption that pre-failure validation automatically survived.
Does the second descriptor slot itself preserve the old state?

Not necessarily. Dual-slot descriptors provide a way to represent and select a pairing; they do not, by their mere existence, preserve the firmware or state to which a descriptor refers. For recovery to use the previously committed pair, its referenced firmware and state must remain available and compatible. If migration changes the only usable copy of that state before activation, an old descriptor alone would not solve the problem.
Then what must be true specifically in the gap between validation and activation?

The effective committed selection must still identify a recoverable compatible pair. Work done on a candidate must not make that selected pair unusable. Recovery must also be able to recognize that the candidate has not been activated, rather than guessing based on how far preparation appeared to progress. Those are conditions the dual-slot approach would have to satisfy; the proposal has not specified the concrete mechanism for satisfying them.
Suppose the candidate descriptor has been written into the other slot, but the activation step has not occurred. Would recovery read it?

Recovery might inspect both slots, but inspection is different from selecting a slot as effective. In the case you describe, merely finding a candidate descriptor should not be enough to promote it. The recovery rule needs to distinguish a prepared candidate from an atomically committed choice, so a power failure before activation does not leave an ambiguous pairing.
What if power fails during activation rather than just before it?

That is another boundary the atomic-commit claim must cover. Recovery would need to identify a complete committed choice and recover the firmware-state pair it names, without combining parts of different pairs. If an interrupted activation can leave an ambiguous or partially effective descriptor, then calling the commit atomic would not be sufficient. The proposal does not specify how that distinction is encoded or made durable.
Am I asking too much of the word “atomic” if I expect it to cover power loss?

No. For this question, atomicity has to be meaningful across the interruption: recovery should observe a coherent committed pair, not a half-switched firmware-state selection. But the word alone is not a mechanism or proof. In particular, atomic descriptor selection and preservation of the firmware and state it selects are both necessary considerations.
Could the recovered pair be the candidate if validation was complete, even though activation had not happened?

The fact of validation alone does not authorize that conclusion. Under a rule where descriptor activation is the commit point, a failure before activation leaves the previously committed pair selected. A different rule for completing a candidate after recovery would need to establish the candidate's integrity and compatibility and define when it becomes committed. Nothing in the question specifies such a rule.
Is there a simple way to state the distinction without assuming a particular descriptor format?

Yes: a candidate may be validated without being committed, and recovery must follow an unambiguous committed selection of a compatible firmware-state pair. For the pre-activation power failure you described, the dual-slot approach works only if the previously committed pair remains recoverable and the candidate is not mistaken for an active pair. That statement leaves the descriptor format open.
What if validation checked the migrated state in memory, but the saved state was not fully written before power failed?

Then the pre-failure validation would not, by itself, prove that a recoverable candidate state exists. Recovery must not select a candidate firmware-state pair merely because an earlier in-memory version passed validation. It needs a compatible pair whose relevant contents are actually available after the failure. Before activation, retaining a recoverable previously committed pair prevents that incomplete candidate from becoming the only option.
Does the same reasoning apply if the candidate firmware is present but the state migration is incomplete?

Yes. A firmware image on its own is not a validated firmware-state pair. If its associated state is incomplete or incompatible, selecting that firmware with the state left by the interrupted migration would fail the pairing requirement. The recovery choice must be a compatible pair, not whichever candidate component happens to be present.
How does this relate to rejecting an incompatible migration atomically?

Validation must not cause an incompatible candidate to become the effective pair. If migration proves incompatible, rejection should leave no partial migration in effect as the committed state. A power failure before activation raises a related but distinct question: even if a candidate had passed validation, recovery must still respect what was committed and preserve access to a compatible pair. Neither case allows a partially prepared candidate to become effective by accident.
And the 1 ms control deadline—is that something recovery after a power failure has to meet?

The 1 ms deadline requirement applies throughout uninterrupted updates. A power failure interrupts operation; the requirement addressed here is to recover a compatible firmware-state pair after an update-time reset. The proposed control island must still meet the 1 ms deadlines while an update proceeds without interruption, including across its normal preparation and commit activity, but this question does not establish deadline continuity through power loss.
Does recovering a compatible pair also prove that no actuator commands were duplicated or skipped at the switch?

No. Descriptor recovery concerns which firmware and state are paired. Sequence-gated actuator writes are the separate proposed safeguard for command consistency during an uninterrupted update. A coherent recovered pair does not, by itself, demonstrate an uninterrupted actuator-command sequence across a power failure, nor does it prove that a normal live switch meets the no-duplicate-or-skip condition.
What is the shortest direct answer to my original power-failure question?

Before descriptor activation, validation must not change the committed pairing. If power fails in that gap, recovery can use the previously committed compatible firmware-state pair—provided it remains intact and the dual-slot commit rule clearly identifies it. An unactivated, even validated, candidate is not automatically the recovered pair.

I have a hypothesis for the reset case: checksummed, schema-validated firmware-state slots with final-write monotonic commit markers let boot recover a compatible pair after every write-boundary reset. Does that state the idea clearly?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It names three distinct safeguards: checksums for detecting damaged slot contents, schema validation for assessing the firmware-state pairing, and a monotonic commit marker written last to distinguish a committed slot from one still being prepared. The claimed outcome is specific: boot can recover a compatible pair after every write-boundary reset. That outcome still needs to be established; it does not follow from the names of the safeguards alone.
Why say “firmware-state slots” rather than just “state slots”?

Because the recovery target is a compatible firmware-state pair. A valid-looking state is insufficient if the firmware selected at boot cannot use it. Calling them firmware-state slots keeps attention on the pairing that boot must validate and recover, without requiring a particular physical layout for the firmware and state.
What work does the checksum do in this hypothesis?

It provides a way for boot to check whether the contents associated with a slot appear intact. That matters if a reset interrupts update writes. A passing checksum is not, on its own, a compatibility judgment: intact contents could still describe a state schema that the paired firmware cannot use.
So the schema-validation part has a different job?

Yes. It addresses whether the state in a candidate pair is suitable for its firmware across a schema change. The hypothesis requires slots to be schema-validated, not merely checksummed. It does not specify the schema rules or the validation procedure, so it should not be read as claiming that a particular validation method has already been demonstrated.
Why must the commit marker be the final write?

The intended distinction is that a slot can be prepared and validated without yet being committed. Writing the marker last would make commitment depend on completion of the preceding work, rather than on the mere presence of some candidate contents. For the hypothesis to hold, that final-write ordering must be meaningful to boot after a write-boundary reset; simply intending to write the marker last would not establish that ordering.
Does “monotonic” mean the marker itself verifies the state migration?

No. Monotonicity concerns the progression of commit markers, so boot can distinguish committed choices according to the proposed commit scheme. It does not substitute for a checksum or schema validation. A marker can indicate a commitment only under rules that also tie it unambiguously to the firmware-state pair being selected.
In the interval after migration validation but before the marker is written, what would boot be expected to do?

Under this hypothesis, the validated candidate has not yet received its final commit marker. Boot would need to recover a compatible pair from a slot already committed, rather than treat validation alone as activation. That requires the previously committed pair to remain recoverable while the candidate is being prepared; the marker cannot restore a previous pair whose contents have been made unusable.
And if the reset occurs immediately after the marker write?

The hypothesis claims recovery at that write boundary too. Boot would need to recognize the newly committed slot and establish that the firmware-state pair it identifies passes the required integrity and schema checks. To justify that outcome, the design would have to show that the contents the marker commits were complete and recoverable when the marker became effective.
Could boot just choose whichever slot has the greatest marker?

The monotonic markers suggest a way to order committed candidates, but marker order alone is not enough to guarantee a compatible pair. Boot would also have to treat the selected slot as a coherent firmware-state pair and apply the integrity and compatibility conditions in the hypothesis. The exact selection rule is not specified by the hypothesis.
What if one slot has a marker but fails its checksum?

Then its marker alone would not establish a recoverable pair. For the hypothesis to cover that reset boundary, boot would need some other recoverable, compatible committed pair, or the design would need to show why that situation cannot arise within the stated failure model. The hypothesis does not yet resolve that case merely by mentioning checksums and markers.
Does the claim cover a reset halfway through an individual write?

It specifically says “after every write-boundary reset.” That identifies resets at boundaries between writes. It does not, without an additional argument, extend the claim to resets partway through a write. Keeping that scope explicit is important when assessing what the hypothesis actually promises.
Is “every” doing significant work there?

Yes. The claim is not just that boot usually recovers, or that recovery works if the reset occurs before preparation begins or after commitment is complete. It covers each write boundary during the update, including boundaries between validation and the final marker write. A justification would need to consider the committed choices available at each such boundary.
Would a checksum prove that firmware and state came from the same candidate?

Not by itself. A checksum can check contents associated with what it covers, but pairing is a separate condition. The hypothesis requires checksummed, schema-validated firmware-state slots; for it to work, boot must be able to identify which firmware and state belong to the same committed slot rather than independently selecting individually intact components.
Am I assuming too much if I say that the marker makes an incompatible migration impossible to commit?

That would be stronger than the marker alone supports. The hypothesis combines a final-write commit marker with schema validation: only a pair that has passed the required validation should reach the committed choice. The marker distinguishes commitment; it does not determine compatibility. The design would need to establish that an incompatible migration cannot become effective through the commit process.
How does this hypothesis relate to atomic rejection of an incompatible migration?

If the migration is incompatible, it must not become a committed effective firmware-state pair, and rejection must not leave a partial migration in effect. In the hypothesized scheme, the absence of a final commit marker on an incompatible candidate could help preserve that distinction. But atomic rejection also depends on keeping an existing compatible pair usable; leaving partially migrated state underneath an older committed marker would not achieve it.
Do the markers change the uninterrupted-update requirements for the 1 ms control island or actuator writes?

No. This hypothesis is about recovering a compatible firmware-state pair after write-boundary resets. It does not demonstrate that an uninterrupted update meets every 1 ms control deadline, nor that actuator commands are neither duplicated nor skipped. The immutable control island and sequence-gated actuator writes remain separate parts of the proposed design whose behavior must be established on their own terms.
What should I be most careful not to claim prematurely?

Do not turn the hypothesis into a completed recovery result. Checksums, schema validation, and final-write monotonic markers describe a plausible structure, but the claim about every write-boundary reset depends on such matters as the recoverability of a previously committed pair, the durability of prepared contents before commitment, and boot's unambiguous interpretation of the marker and its paired contents. Those are conditions to establish, not observations already supplied.
Can we phrase the hypothesis compactly while keeping that uncertainty?

A compact version is: “Hypothesis: If checksummed, schema-validated firmware-state slots retain a recoverable committed pair and use monotonic commit markers written last, boot can select a compatible firmware-state pair after every write-boundary reset.” The added condition makes clear why an uncommitted or incomplete candidate need not become the recovery choice, while keeping the conclusion a hypothesis rather than a proven result.

For the power-failure question, I want a concrete plan: specify the ordering of validation and marker writes, inject resets at every flash-write boundary, and verify that boot selects a compatible committed firmware-state pair. Is that the right scope?

Yes. That is a plan for examining the recovery behavior, not a claim that recovery has already been demonstrated. First make the intended ordering explicit; then interrupt the update at each flash-write boundary; then check the pair boot selects after each reset. The required observation in every case is a pair that is both committed and compatible.
Why specify the ordering before injecting resets?

Without a defined ordering, it would be unclear what each reset interrupted or which pair should count as committed at that point. The specification should distinguish validation of a candidate from the marker write that makes a choice effective. It gives the boundary checks something definite to evaluate, especially between validation and descriptor activation.
Does the plan require us to prescribe a particular validation algorithm?

No particular algorithm is stated. The plan calls for specifying how validation is ordered relative to marker writes, so that a candidate is not treated as committed merely because validation occurred. How compatibility is determined may need definition in the design, but this plan does not supply a specific test or state schema.
What should “every flash-write boundary” mean when we carry out the reset injections?

It means the planned checks should cover each boundary between flash writes in the update sequence being evaluated, rather than a few selected moments such as only before and after the update. The order has to be specified so those boundaries can be identified. This wording does not, on its own, claim coverage of a reset partway through an individual write.
Would the boundary immediately after validation be included?

If that point is a flash-write boundary in the specified update sequence, yes. It is particularly relevant to the question of a failure between migration validation and descriptor activation. The test would ask what boot selects after a reset there; it should not assume that validation alone committed the candidate.
And do we also check the boundaries around the marker write?

Yes, where those are flash-write boundaries in the specified sequence. Checking on either side of the marker write helps distinguish a prepared candidate from a committed choice. The plan is to observe boot's actual selection after each injected reset, not to infer recovery solely from the intended write order.
Is it enough to see that boot starts successfully?

No. The verification target is more specific: boot must select a compatible committed firmware-state pair. A successful start, by itself, would not establish that the selected state matches its firmware or that the selection was committed rather than an incomplete candidate.
Should we verify the firmware and state separately?

They need to be checked as a pair. The plan is not satisfied by showing that one firmware item and one state item each appear usable independently. Boot must select a committed pairing in which the firmware and state are compatible with each other.
What does “committed” add to “compatible” in that check?

It rules out treating a merely prepared or validated candidate as the recovery choice without the specified commit step. Compatibility answers whether the firmware and state can go together; commitment answers whether that pair became an effective choice under the defined marker-write ordering. The verification calls for both.
If boot chooses a compatible candidate that was validated but not marked committed, would that count as passing?

Not against this plan as stated. The planned check is that boot selects a compatible *committed* pair. If the specification defines marker activation as the commit event, a candidate selected before that event would fail the commitment part of the check, even if its firmware and state happened to be compatible.
Do I need to predict in advance which slot boot will select at each boundary?

The specification needs to make clear which choices count as committed at each boundary, so the observation can be judged. The plan's stated outcome is a compatible committed pair, not necessarily a named slot at every point. Avoid assuming that whichever slot looks newest is acceptable without checking commitment and compatibility.
What if there are several flash writes associated with preparation? Can I test only the last one before the marker?

That would narrow the stated plan. “Every flash-write boundary” includes boundaries throughout the specified flash-write sequence, not only the one closest to the marker. The purpose is to check recovery from each interruption point where the amount of completed update work may differ.
Is a reset injection here meant to show what happens during an uninterrupted live update?

No. These injections deliberately interrupt the update to examine reset recovery. They do not, by themselves, verify that an uninterrupted update meets each 1 ms control deadline or avoids duplicated and skipped actuator commands. This plan is focused on boot selecting a compatible committed firmware-state pair after the injected resets.
Could we describe the checks as proving the dual-slot idea works?

That would be premature before carrying them out and assessing their coverage. The plan specifies what to define, where to inject resets, and what to verify afterward. If the observations meet the check at every specified flash-write boundary, they would support the recovery claim for that tested boundary scope; the plan alone is not a result.
What would constitute a clear failure of the planned verification?

At any injected flash-write boundary, boot selecting a pair that is incompatible, or selecting an uncommitted candidate as though it were committed, would fail the stated check. So would an outcome where boot cannot identify a compatible committed pair. Those are ways of applying the verification criterion, not predictions about what the test will find.
Should the ordering specification cover the gap between validating the migration and activating its descriptor explicitly?

Yes. That gap motivates the plan. State clearly what remains committed after validation and before the marker write that activates a descriptor, then inject a reset at each applicable flash-write boundary in that interval. Verification should examine the pair boot actually selects, rather than assuming that a validated candidate or a prior pair will necessarily be chosen.
Can I phrase the plan in one sentence without making it sound like the tests are already complete?

Specify the ordering of migration validation and commit-marker writes, inject resets at every flash-write boundary in that sequence, and after each reset verify that boot selects a compatible committed firmware-state pair.

I’m ready to run SlotCrash-1. The activity is to reset after each firmware, migrated-state, CRC, and commit-marker write, then assert that boot loads matching committed generations. How should I describe the scope?

Describe SlotCrash-1 as a write-boundary reset activity. For each firmware write, migrated-state write, CRC write, and commit-marker write in the update sequence, inject a reset immediately afterward and check what boot loads. The assertion is that the loaded firmware and state belong to matching committed generations. This describes what to do and check, not an outcome already observed.
Why name each kind of write instead of just saying “reset throughout the update”?

Naming them makes the intended interruption points explicit. A reset after a firmware write may leave different completed work than one after a migrated-state, CRC, or commit-marker write. “Throughout” could be read as a few representative resets; SlotCrash-1 calls for a reset after each write in those categories.
If there are multiple firmware writes, do I reset only after the last one?

No. “After each firmware write” includes each such write, not just the final firmware write. The same reading applies to each migrated-state, CRC, and commit-marker write. Each reset point gets its own boot-selection assertion.
What exactly does “matching committed generations” require?

It requires boot to load firmware and state that belong together as a committed generation. Loading firmware from one generation with migrated state from another would not meet the assertion, even if both items were individually readable. Nor would loading a matching candidate generation suffice if it had not been committed.
So I should not treat a passing CRC as proof that the boot choice is correct?

Correct. A CRC can help check the contents it covers, but the SlotCrash-1 assertion is about boot’s selected pair. The firmware and state must match, and their generation must be committed. A CRC alone does not establish either part of that pairing and commitment check.
What is the point of resetting right after a CRC write?

That boundary checks the behavior when a CRC write has completed but a later commit-marker write may not have occurred. It lets the activity distinguish completed preparation from a committed selection. SlotCrash-1 should check the pair boot actually loads at that point, rather than assume the CRC write activated the candidate.
And the reset immediately after a commit-marker write checks the other side of that distinction?

Yes. It checks boot selection after that marker write has completed. The assertion remains the same: boot must load matching committed generations. For the uninterrupted-update path, I propose staging firmware asynchronously, then switching at 1-ms tick boundaries using prevalidated state buffers and single-writer, sequence-gated actuator commits. How do those pieces fit together?

They separate preparation from the time-critical transition. Firmware staging happens asynchronously rather than being treated as work that must be completed within a control tick. The proposed switch occurs at a 1-ms tick boundary and uses a state buffer that has already been validated. At the actuator boundary, a single writer and sequence-gated commits are intended to preserve the command sequence as control changes over. It is a proposal for meeting the uninterrupted-update requirements, not yet evidence that it meets every 1 ms deadline or avoids every duplicate and skipped command.
Does staging firmware asynchronously mean the switch itself is asynchronous?

No. The proposal distinguishes the two: firmware is staged asynchronously, while the switch is tied to a 1-ms tick boundary. Preparation need not be treated as part of the boundary event. The boundary is the proposed point at which control changes over using already prevalidated state.
Am I saying the firmware has to be staged in exactly one millisecond?

No. The 1-ms value identifies the tick boundaries for switching and the control-deadline context. It does not give a completion time for asynchronous firmware staging. The timing requirement is that staging and switching must not cause control to miss its 1 ms deadlines during an uninterrupted update.
Why insist on a tick boundary for the switch?

It gives the transition a defined relationship to the control cycle, rather than allowing a changeover at an arbitrary point within one. That can help make the handoff understandable, but choosing a boundary is not itself proof of correct timing or command sequencing. The work performed at that boundary must still fit without missing the applicable 1 ms deadline.
Could I say a tick-boundary switch guarantees there is no control interruption?

That would be too strong. It specifies *when* the switch is intended to occur, not how long the transition takes or whether all control work remains timely. The design must still establish that every 1 ms control deadline is met throughout the uninterrupted update.
What does “prevalidated state buffers” contribute?

It means the state buffer to be used for the switch has been validated before the switch, rather than making the tick-boundary transition depend on doing its validation at that moment. This matters when the state schema changes: the proposed transition should use state suitable for the firmware taking over. The proposal does not specify a validation method, the number of buffers, or their storage layout.
Does prevalidation mean any schema migration must be accepted?

No. A buffer that cannot be validated as suitable must not be treated as a prevalidated input to the switch. The broader requirement is to reject incompatible state migrations atomically. The phrase “prevalidated state buffers” does not define which migrations are compatible or turn an incompatible migration into an acceptable one.
Would it be fair to describe validation as taking place outside the 1-ms tick?

You can say it takes place *before the switch at the tick boundary*. The proposal does not give a precise schedule for validation relative to every tick. Its important distinction is that the switch uses state buffers already validated, rather than depending on uncompleted validation during the changeover.
Are the buffers necessarily copies of the controller’s entire state?

That is not specified. “State buffers” names what the switch uses, but it does not say how much state each contains or how it is represented. Avoid claiming a particular copying strategy from this proposal alone.
How do I explain “single-writer” without saying only one firmware version can ever produce a command?

Describe it at the actuator commit point: actuator commands have one writer responsible for committing them. That does not require a claim about how many components may calculate or prepare a prospective command. The proposed restriction concerns who can make a command effective at the actuator boundary, particularly across the switch.
What if both sides of a switch are ready with an actuator command?

The single-writer, sequence-gated commit rule is meant to prevent two independently effective writes from creating a duplicate during that handoff. The proposal does not specify which prospective command is chosen or an exact arbitration procedure. It still needs to ensure that the intended command sequence is neither duplicated nor skipped.
Does single-writer alone prevent a command from being skipped?

No. Having only one writer avoids competing effective writers, but that writer could still omit an intended command. Sequence gating also needs to be considered against both sides of the requirement: it must not allow duplicates, and the overall commit process must not skip commands. Neither label alone proves the resulting sequence is complete.
Could sequence gating just reject anything that arrives out of order?

It can be described as conditioning commits on their position in the intended sequence, but simply discarding an unexpected command might create a skip. The proposal does not define the gate’s precise behavior. What matters is that actuator commits preserve the intended sequence through the switch without duplicate or omitted commands.
Does this imply exactly one actuator write at every 1-ms tick boundary?

No. The proposal names 1-ms tick boundaries for switching and sequence-gated actuator commits; it does not set an actuator-write rate. The requirement is to meet 1 ms control deadlines and avoid duplicated or skipped actuator commands, not to infer one command per tick.
How does the prevalidated buffer relate to the firmware being staged asynchronously?

They are the two inputs the switch needs to treat coherently: staged firmware and state already validated for the proposed transition. Staging the firmware does not by itself make an associated state buffer suitable, and a validated buffer does not by itself make the switch timely. The proposal brings them together at the 1-ms tick-boundary switch without defining the internal preparation procedure.
Could the switch happen as soon as firmware staging ends, even if that is between ticks?

Not as this proposal is phrased. Completing asynchronous staging would make the firmware available for a proposed switch, but the switch itself is specified to occur at a 1-ms tick boundary using prevalidated state buffers. Staging completion and switch timing are separate conditions.
What if the state buffer is not prevalidated by the intended tick boundary?

Then it would not meet the proposal’s condition for switching with a prevalidated state buffer at that boundary. The proposal does not specify a fallback scheduling rule or require a switch at a particular tick. It is better not to claim that an unvalidated buffer can be used just to meet an anticipated switch time.
Does the proposal specify how to recover if a reset occurs during staging or switching?

No. It describes asynchronous staging, a tick-boundary switch, prevalidated state buffers, and single-writer, sequence-gated actuator commits. The broader live-update goal still requires recovery of a compatible firmware-state pair after any update-time reset, but this proposal does not by itself define that reset-recovery mechanism.
Should I describe actuator consistency and deadline preservation as one check?

Keep them distinct. A switch at a 1-ms tick boundary could still be too slow and miss a control deadline. A timely switch could still duplicate or skip an actuator command. The proposal’s staging and boundary choices address when work and changeover occur, while the single-writer, sequence-gated commits address the command handoff. Both outcomes have to be established.
Is it accurate to say prevalidation alone ensures the state schema stays compatible after any reset?

No. Prevalidation concerns the state buffer used for the proposed switch. Recovering a compatible firmware-state pair after a reset is a separate obligation; a reset may interrupt update work at a different point. The proposal should not be presented as a complete reset-recovery argument merely because it uses prevalidated buffers.
What is the most concise way to state the proposal without turning it into a demonstrated result?

“Proposal: Stage firmware asynchronously, switch at 1-ms tick boundaries using prevalidated state buffers, and commit actuator commands through a single writer with sequence gating.” The intended outcomes are uninterrupted 1 ms control deadlines and no duplicated or skipped actuator commands, but those outcomes still need to be established for the proposed switch.
Can a tick-boundary handoff preserve every 1-ms deadline and exactly one actuator write per sequence during state-schema conversion?

That is the central question for the uninterrupted-update handoff. A tick boundary gives the changeover a defined point, but it does not by itself prove either property. The design must show that control meets every 1 ms deadline through the handoff and that each intended actuator-command sequence has one effective write—neither a duplicate nor an omission—while firmware and state change together.
Does “exactly one actuator write per sequence” mean one write every 1 ms?

No. The 1 ms figure applies to control deadlines. “Exactly one per sequence” concerns the identity of an intended actuator command: its sequence must not be committed twice or skipped. Nothing in the question establishes that every control tick necessarily produces an actuator write.
Why isn't switching at the tick boundary enough to protect the deadline?

The boundary specifies when the handoff occurs, not how much time its work takes or whether control can still finish on time. If the changeover delays the control work due for a tick, identifying that delay as a boundary operation would not make the missed 1 ms deadline acceptable.
If the handoff briefly pauses control but the next tick runs normally, would that meet the question?

Not if that pause causes a control deadline to be missed. The question asks whether the handoff can preserve *every* 1-ms deadline, not whether timing returns to normal afterward or meets the deadline on average.
Where does state-schema conversion enter the timing question?

A schema change means the firmware taking over needs state it can use. If conversion work is required at the handoff, that work could affect whether the control deadline is met. Using a prevalidated state buffer is a proposed way to avoid making the tick-boundary switch depend on unfinished conversion or validation, but the question remains whether the complete handoff actually meets every deadline.
Are we assuming the entire conversion takes place inside one 1-ms interval?

No. The question does not specify when conversion runs or how long it takes. The proposed switch uses prevalidated state buffers; that keeps preparation conceptually distinct from the boundary switch. What must be preserved during an uninterrupted update is the 1 ms control deadline, wherever conversion work is performed.
So a prevalidated buffer doesn't answer the deadline question on its own?

Correct. It addresses whether suitable state is ready for the new firmware, but it does not establish that selecting it, changing control over, and continuing control all fit within the deadline. Readiness of the state and timeliness of the handoff are separate conditions.
Does prevalidation answer the actuator-write question?

Not by itself. A suitable state buffer helps the firmware operate on the intended state schema, but it does not determine which side of the handoff makes an actuator write effective. The single-writer, sequence-gated commit proposal addresses that separate command-consistency issue.
What would go wrong if both sides of the handoff wrote an actuator command with the same sequence?

There would be a duplicated actuator write for that sequence, violating the “exactly one” condition. A tick-boundary switch alone does not exclude that possibility; the effective actuator-commit path must prevent both sides from committing the same sequence.
What if neither side writes it because each assumes the other will?

Then that sequence is skipped, which also violates the condition. Preventing two writes is only half the task. The handoff needs to preserve ownership of each intended command so that one effective write occurs for its sequence.
Can single-writer actuator commits solve both problems automatically?

Not automatically. A single writer rules out competing effective writers, but it still needs to commit the intended sequences without omissions. Sequence gating can constrain which sequence becomes effective, yet the combined behavior must be assessed for both duplicates and skips during the changeover.
Does “exactly one” count a command calculated before the switch but written after it?

The relevant count is effective actuator writes for that command's sequence, not which side calculated it or precisely when it was prepared. The question does not specify a rule for assigning such a command to either side. Whatever the handoff rule is, it must produce one effective write for each intended sequence while maintaining the 1 ms control deadlines.
If a duplicate is suppressed by sequence gating, have we proved the handoff is consistent?

No. Suppressing a duplicate addresses one possible violation. You would still need to know that the intended write for that sequence occurred and that no other sequence was skipped. The timing requirement also remains independent: sequence consistency does not excuse a late control cycle.
Could we meet the actuator condition but still fail because conversion delayed a tick?

Yes. Exactly one effective write per intended sequence would not demonstrate that every 1-ms control deadline was preserved. The question asks for both properties during the state-schema change, so a deadline miss would leave it unanswered in the affirmative.
And could we meet all the deadlines but still fail at the actuator boundary?
Yes. Finishing each control cycle on time would not rule out a duplicated or skipped actuator write during the handoff. Deadline preservation and actuator-command continuity must each be established.
Do we need to claim that conversion and the handoff happen at the very same instant?

No. The question concerns whether the tick-boundary handoff preserves both properties *during* a state-schema conversion. It does not prescribe simultaneous conversion and switching. In the proposal, the switch uses prevalidated state buffers, so it is important not to silently move an unspecified amount of conversion work into the boundary event.
What if the state isn't ready when a tick boundary arrives?

Then that boundary would not have the prevalidated state buffer the proposed switch calls for. The question does not require a switch at a particular tick, and it would not be sound to assume an unready buffer can be used simply to switch on schedule. Control still has to meet its 1 ms deadlines while the update remains uninterrupted.
Does this question also settle what happens after a reset during the schema change?

No. This asks about tick-boundary handoff, deadlines, and actuator writes during an uninterrupted update involving state-schema conversion. Recovery of a compatible firmware-state pair after an update-time reset is a separate obligation; answering this handoff question would not, by itself, answer the reset question.
How can I express the two things that need to be demonstrated without claiming they have already happened?

Ask whether, across the tick-boundary switch using the converted state, every control cycle still meets its 1 ms deadline and every intended actuator-command sequence receives exactly one effective write. That formulation keeps the timing and command-sequence checks distinct and treats their success as an open question.
Is this a fair short version: “Does a tick-boundary switch with prevalidated state prevent deadline misses and double writes?”

It captures part of the question, but include skipped writes as well as double writes. A closer version is: “During state-schema conversion, can a tick-boundary handoff using prevalidated state preserve every 1-ms control deadline and exactly one actuator write per intended sequence, with neither duplicates nor skips?”

Is the bound “less than 40 µs” or “no more than 40 µs”?
No more than 40 µs. The symbol ≤ includes a swap lasting exactly 40 µs. Calling the bound “less than 40 µs” would exclude that case and change the hypothesis.
Does a tick-boundary swap mean the entire control cycle can be deferred until the next tick?

No. The hypothesis says the swap occurs at a tick boundary while 1-ms control deadlines are preserved. Deferring due control work and catching up later would not establish that every deadline was met.
What does “exactly one actuator commit per sequence” add to the timing claim?

It adds a separate consistency condition. For each intended actuator-command sequence, there must be one effective commit—not two and not zero—across the handoff. A swap could meet its ≤40-µs limit and still fail that condition, just as an orderly commit sequence would not excuse a missed 1-ms deadline.
Does that mean exactly one actuator commit every millisecond?

No. “Per sequence” identifies the unit being counted; it does not establish one sequence, or one actuator commit, per 1-ms tick. The hypothesis connects the tick interval to control deadlines and connects the exactly-one rule to each intended actuator sequence.
Could I claim that prevalidated shadow state by itself prevents duplicate actuator commits?

No. Prevalidated shadow state addresses the state presented at the switch. Exactly one actuator commit per sequence is a distinct property of the handoff. The hypothesis asserts both together, but it does not say that state prevalidation alone enforces commit uniqueness or prevents omissions.
Is the exactly-one condition satisfied if two writes are attempted but one is later undone?

The hypothesis is about exactly one actuator *commit* per sequence. A description of attempted writes and an undo would not, on its own, establish that exactly one commit became effective. What if there are zero commits for a particular sequence but all subsequent sequences have one?

That would not satisfy “exactly one actuator commit per sequence.” The missing sequence is a skip, even if subsequent commits are individually unique. The hypothesis requires continuity as well as protection against duplicates.
Does the hypothesis specify which firmware side owns a command at the swap?

No. It specifies the desired effective outcome—exactly one actuator commit per sequence—but does not define an ownership or arbitration rule at the tick boundary. Adding a particular handoff mechanism would go beyond this hypothesis.
Can I say the state-schema conversion is compatible because its shadow state is prevalidated?

You can say the hypothesis calls for converted shadow state to be prevalidated before use. It does not provide the validation criteria or establish that any particular conversion passed them. “Prevalidated” is a condition of the proposed handoff, not a reported test result.
What if the converted shadow state isn't prevalidated when the swap would occur?

Then the stated conditions of the hypothesis have not been met for that swap. The hypothesis does not authorize switching with unvalidated state, nor does it require a switch at a particular tick. Is ≤40 µs a measured worst-case swap time?
Not as stated. It is a bound in the hypothesis. No measurement or timing result is supplied here, so it should not be reported as an observed worst case.
Does this hypothesis also establish recovery after an update-time reset?

No. It concerns an uninterrupted tick-boundary handoff during state-schema conversion: prevalidated shadow state, a ≤40-µs swap, 1-ms deadlines, and exactly one actuator commit per sequence. Recovery of a compatible firmware-state pair after a reset is a separate requirement, not an outcome demonstrated by this hypothesis.

For the actuator path, I propose a fixed 1-ms actuator dispatcher with fenced firmware producers, per-tick command selection, and fallback commands during handoff. How should I explain the design?

Explain it as separating command production from the time-critical actuator dispatch. Firmware producers may supply commands, but a fixed dispatcher operates on the 1-ms cadence and selects the command for each tick. Fencing limits which producer can contribute across the handoff, while fallback commands provide a proposed selection when the handoff would otherwise leave the dispatcher without a suitable producer command. This is a proposal for preserving deadlines and actuator consistency, not a demonstrated result.
Does “fixed” mean the firmware being updated can never change?

No. It describes the actuator dispatcher as the stable part of this proposed handoff. Firmware producers can change as part of the update; the dispatcher remains fixed while it selects and issues actuator commands. The proposal does not specify whether the dispatcher could ever be changed in some other operation.
Why make the dispatcher operate every 1 ms?

That cadence aligns command selection with the controller’s 1 ms control timing. It gives the handoff a recurring, defined point at which to select an actuator command. The design would still need to establish that dispatcher and update activity allow every 1 ms control deadline to be met.
Does a 1-ms dispatcher require exactly one physical actuator write on every tick?

The proposal says the dispatcher has a fixed 1-ms cadence and performs per-tick command selection; it does not separately define the number of physical writes per tick. The consistency requirement is that intended actuator commands are neither duplicated nor skipped. Avoid turning the dispatcher cadence into an unstated command-rate rule.
What do you mean by “firmware producers” in this proposal?

They are the firmware-side sources of prospective actuator commands. Calling them producers distinguishes supplying a command from making it effective at the actuator. The proposal does not specify how many producers exist, how they generate commands, or how they communicate with the dispatcher.
And what does it mean to fence a producer?

Conceptually, fencing prevents a producer that is not authorized for the relevant handoff interval from influencing the effective command selection. That matters if commands could be offered from different sides of a firmware transition. The proposal does not specify a fencing mechanism or the precise rule for transferring authorization.
Would fencing one producer automatically prevent duplicate actuator commands?

Not automatically. Fencing addresses which producers can contribute, but duplicate prevention also depends on how the dispatcher selects and issues effective commands. The full proposal would need to ensure a command is not issued twice while also ensuring an intended command is not omitted.
Could both producers calculate the same prospective command without violating the actuator requirement?

Prospective commands are different from effective actuator commands. The relevant question is what the dispatcher selects and issues, not whether more than one producer calculated something. The proposed fencing and per-tick selection are meant to keep the handoff from turning competing proposals into duplicate effective commands, but their exact behavior is not specified.
What does “per-tick command selection” add beyond having a dispatcher?

It makes selection an explicit responsibility at each 1-ms dispatcher tick. Rather than assuming that whichever producer writes first controls the actuator, the dispatcher determines what command is selected for that tick. The proposal does not prescribe the selection criteria or a particular priority between producers.
Does that imply the dispatcher picks the newest command?

No. Nothing here defines “newest” as the selection rule. The proposal calls for per-tick selection among available command sources, subject to producer fencing and the handoff arrangement. A concrete selection rule would need to preserve the intended actuator-command sequence without compromising deadlines.
How do fallback commands fit in?

They are the proposed command option during handoff if an ordinary producer command is not suitable for selection at a tick. Their role is to avoid leaving the dispatcher without a command choice simply because ownership is changing. The proposal does not define the fallback command values, how they are chosen, or when they are appropriate.
Can we assume the fallback command repeats the last actuator value?

No. “Fallback commands” does not specify their content. Repeating a previous value would be a particular policy, and it could not be assumed to satisfy the no-duplicate-or-skip requirement without defining what counts as an intended command. Keep the fallback’s purpose explicit without inventing its value.
If a fallback is selected, is that automatically evidence no command was skipped?

No. A fallback provides a possible command during the handoff, but the design still has to establish that each intended command sequence is handled correctly. Selecting something on a tick does not, by itself, show that an intended actuator command was neither omitted nor duplicated.
Could the fallback and a firmware-produced command both be issued for one tick?

That would be a situation the proposed dispatcher should avoid if it would duplicate an effective actuator command. Per-tick selection should produce an unambiguous effective choice, but the proposal does not spell out the selection or commit rules. It must be assessed against the requirement to avoid both duplicates and skips.
When the handoff finishes, does the proposal say precisely when fallback selection ends?

No. It says fallback commands are available during handoff, not which tick starts or ends their use. Fencing, producer availability, and command selection would need a coherent transition rule, but no particular boundary rule is stated here.
Would a fixed dispatcher let the firmware update take as long as it wants without affecting timing?

That does not follow. Separating dispatch from firmware producers may help isolate the 1-ms path, but the uninterrupted update must still meet every 1 ms control deadline. The proposal gives a structure for that objective; it does not establish that all update work has no timing effect.
Is the dispatcher the same thing as the state-schema conversion mechanism?

No. This proposal concerns selection and dispatch of actuator commands during a firmware handoff. It does not specify how state is converted, how a migration is validated or rejected, or how boot recovers a compatible firmware-state pair after a reset. Those obligations remain part of the larger update design.
What if the new firmware producer has no command ready on the handoff tick?

The proposed fallback commands give the dispatcher a possible choice during handoff, rather than requiring an unready producer to supply a command. Whether that choice preserves the intended command sequence depends on rules not given here. The dispatcher must still meet its timing and actuator-consistency obligations.
Should I describe fencing as permanently disabling the prior producer?

No. The proposal says the firmware producers are fenced, but does not specify whether a fence is permanent or how authorization changes. It is enough to say fencing constrains which producer may affect the dispatcher’s effective command selection during the handoff.
What are the distinct claims we would eventually need to check for this proposal?

You would need to establish that control still meets every 1 ms deadline during an uninterrupted update and that the actuator’s effective command sequence has neither duplicates nor skips through the handoff. The dispatcher cadence, producer fencing, per-tick selection, and fallback commands describe a proposed way to achieve those outcomes; naming the components does not verify them.
Can I say the fallback makes a skipped actuator command impossible?

Not as stated. The no-skips property has to be established for the effective sequence, not inferred from the mere presence of a fallback option.
How would you state the proposal in one sentence without promising that it already works?

“Proposal: Use a fixed 1-ms actuator dispatcher that selects commands per tick from fenced firmware producers, with fallback commands available during handoff, to support uninterrupted control timing and consistent actuator commands.” Whether it actually meets every deadline and avoids duplicated or skipped commands remains to be established.

What makes a producer stale?

In this question, a producer is stale if it is no longer authorized to influence effective actuator commands after the relevant handoff. That can include a command it prepared earlier but presents too late. The question does not specify how authorization is represented or precisely when it changes.
If an old command arrives on the first tick after the switch, why not use it instead of a fallback?

Its arrival does not by itself show that it is authorized for that tick or that its state assumptions still fit the handoff. The question does not establish that an old-producer command, a new-producer command, or a fallback is always the right choice at that boundary.
Could the dispatcher accept an old producer’s command as long as the command was computed before the handoff?

That timing alone is not enough to decide. What matters is whether the command is eligible to become the effective command for the tick under a coherent handoff rule. A command computed before the handoff could still arrive after its producer has become stale. The proposal does not define an eligibility rule based solely on computation time.
Is fencing mainly about preventing two producers from writing to the actuator?

That is an important part of it: stale producers must not bypass the dispatcher and create a competing effective write. Fencing also concerns which prospective commands the dispatcher is permitted to consider. Even if the dispatcher is the only effective writer, selecting a stale producer’s command without an authorization rule would leave the handoff ambiguous.
What if both the old and new firmware offer commands for that first tick?

The dispatcher would need one unambiguous effective selection rather than treating both offers as actuator writes. Fencing determines which producer is eligible, and per-tick selection determines the command to issue. The question does not supply a priority between the old and new producers, so it would be premature to name one as the winner.
And if neither offers a command on time?

That is the situation fallback commands are intended to address during handoff. The dispatcher would need a defined choice it can make within the 1-ms timing constraint. But the mere availability of a fallback does not establish that its content is safe or that using it preserves the intended actuator-command sequence.
Can I call any available command a safe fallback?

No. Availability is not safety. A safe fallback has to be suitable for the controller and the handoff condition; no command value or safety policy is specified here. It would be misleading to label an arbitrary old command, a repeated command, or an arbitrary new command safe without such a rule.
Would repeating the last actuator command be the obvious fallback?

That is one possible policy to consider conceptually, but this question does not establish that repeating the last command is safe. It could also be mistaken for a duplicate if command identity and sequencing are not handled correctly. The supplied proposal says there are fallback commands during handoff; it does not define their values.
Does choosing a fallback solve the skipped-command problem?

Not automatically. The dispatcher might make a choice for the tick while an intended firmware-produced command is still lost or counted incorrectly. The handoff rule needs to distinguish the selected fallback from any late producer offer so that an intended actuator sequence is neither issued twice nor silently omitted. Whether a particular fallback satisfies that condition remains open.
What happens if the new firmware’s first command arrives just after the dispatcher has selected a fallback?

The late arrival must not become a second effective command for the same selection. At the same time, simply discarding it without regard to the intended sequence could cause an omission. The question calls for a rule that handles that timing boundary coherently; it does not specify the rule or claim that a particular late arrival has occurred.
So should a fence apply to commands as well as to the producer that submitted them?

Conceptually, the dispatcher has to judge an offered command’s eligibility for the tick, not merely recognize its producer’s name. A command that was eligible at one point should not automatically remain eligible after the handoff changes who may contribute. That describes the responsibility of fencing without prescribing an implementation.
Is it possible to keep the dispatcher on time but still make the wrong selection?

Yes. A selection can be made within the 1-ms deadline yet use an ineligible stale command, duplicate a sequence, omit an intended sequence, or use a fallback whose safety has not been established. Deadline preservation and actuator-command consistency both matter.
If the new firmware is late, can the dispatcher wait for it beyond the tick boundary?

Not if waiting causes a 1-ms control deadline to be missed. The proposed fixed dispatcher has to make its selection within the control timing constraint. How it handles a missing new-producer command—particularly which fallback is safe—is the open part of your question.
Does “safe command” mean only that the command is not duplicated?

No. Avoiding a duplicate is a sequencing condition, not a complete definition of safety. The question gives no actuator-specific safe value or policy. A suitable choice would have to respect the intended actuator sequence and the controller’s safety requirements, without assuming a particular command is safe merely because it is unique.
Would a fence that blocks every old-producer command as soon as the handoff starts settle this?

It would address one route by which a stale producer could affect the actuator, but it would not decide what the dispatcher selects if the new producer misses its first tick. Nor would it alone prove that no intended command is skipped. The fence boundary and the fallback selection have to work together.

Ask: “At each 1-ms dispatcher tick across the handoff, which producer commands remain eligible, and what defined safe fallback can be selected if the new producer has no timely first command, while ensuring stale offers cannot cause duplicated or skipped actuator commands?” That keeps authorization, selection, timing, and the unresolved meaning of a safe fallback visible.

Arrival time alone would not establish that the offering producer’s epoch is authorized.
