That separation matters if the candidate must be rejected: the proposed outcome is to retain the previous committed pair, not expose a partly migrated candidate.
Does “shadow slot” necessarily mean a complete second copy of every firmware and state item?

No. The proposal names shadow slots for migrations but does not specify their physical layout, capacity, or whether they contain complete copies of everything. The relevant distinction is between candidate migration work and the committed pair that remains effective until activation.
Why call the migration schema-typed?

Because the conversion must be understood in terms of the state schema it starts from and the schema the candidate is meant to satisfy. A candidate should not become effective merely because migration work completed; its resulting state has to be suitable for the firmware-state pairing proposed for activation. The proposal does not specify schema identifiers, fields, or conversion rules.
Does a schema-typed migration automatically establish that its result is compatible?

No. Being schema-typed makes the expected types explicit; it does not establish that every candidate satisfies them or passes the actuator-invariant checks. The proposal deliberately has a rejection path before activation.
What does “bounded” require me to specify?

A concrete design would need to say what limit applies to migration work so it cannot run without a defined bound. This proposal does not give a numerical limit or say whether the bound is expressed as time, work, or another measure. Do not present a particular bound as already chosen.
Can I say the entire migration completes within one 1-ms control tick?

Not from this proposal. The controller’s uninterrupted-update goal calls for meeting every 1 ms control deadline, but “bounded migration” does not mean the complete conversion takes no more than 1 ms. Its scheduling and bound would need to coexist with timely control; neither a one-tick conversion nor a measured deadline outcome is stated here.
Why distinguish the migration bound from the control deadline?

They constrain different things. The migration bound limits the candidate conversion work as specified by the design. The 1-ms deadline concerns continuing control during an uninterrupted update. A migration can have a defined bound and still interfere with a deadline unless the full design prevents that interference.
Are actuator invariants just another name for schema types?

No. Schema typing concerns the form and compatibility of state. Actuator invariants concern conditions that must hold for actuator consistency when the migrated state is used. The proposal requires rejection on actuator-invariant failure before activation; it does not define the individual invariants or imply that passing schema checks proves they pass.
Could you give a concrete actuator invariant to put into the proposal?

No particular invariant is supplied, so naming one as a requirement would add an unsupported design fact. It is accurate to say that the invariants must be specified and checked before activation, and that failure of any applicable actuator-invariant check rejects the candidate.
Does rejecting on an invariant failure mean an incompatible state can briefly become effective and then be rolled back?

No. “Reject ... before activation” rules out making that failed candidate effective first and correcting it afterward. The proposed outcome is to keep the previous committed firmware-state pair while declining to activate the candidate.
Can migration work still have occurred in the shadow slot when we reject it?

Yes. Rejection before activation does not imply that no candidate work took place. It means that work must not become the effective migrated state after an actuator-invariant failure. The proposal does not specify whether or when rejected shadow-slot contents are erased.
What exactly remains previous when the migration is rejected?

The previous *committed firmware-state pair* is retained. The proposal does not merely say to keep the old state while activating new firmware, or to keep old firmware while using candidate state. The unit retained is the pair.
Does retaining the previous pair require choosing a particular slot identifier?

No slot identifier is given. The requirement is about the effective committed choice, not which physical slot holds it. A concrete implementation would have to identify that pair reliably, but the proposal does not specify the descriptor or selection format.
If the candidate is schema-typed and all migration work finishes, must it be activated?

No. Completion of migration work is not the same as permission to activate. The actuator-invariant checks are a separate preactivation condition, and the proposal does not state that they are the only possible conditions on a candidate.
What if an invariant check fails only after activation?

That would not be the rejection behavior proposed here. The proposal specifically calls for rejecting actuator-invariant failures *before* activation. It does not give a post-activation repair procedure or claim that such a procedure would be equivalent.
Does this make incompatible state migration rejection atomic?

It proposes an important part of atomic rejection: perform candidate migration in a shadow slot, and if an actuator invariant fails, leave the previous committed pair effective instead of making partial candidate changes effective. Whether a concrete implementation achieves atomic rejection under every relevant interruption still has to be established; the proposal itself is not that verification.
Would it be accurate to say that the previous pair cannot change in any way while a shadow migration runs?

That is stronger than the proposal states. It requires retaining the previous committed pair if the candidate fails an actuator invariant. It does not define all runtime state behavior during migration or assert that every aspect of the operating controller is frozen.
Is a shadow-slot migration necessarily the same operation as switching which pair the dispatcher uses?

No. Migration prepares candidate state; activation is the separate point at which a candidate firmware-state pair could become effective. The proposal relies on keeping those stages distinct so an actuator-invariant failure can be rejected before activation. It does not specify how activation is synchronized with dispatch.
Can I claim that this proposal by itself prevents duplicated or skipped actuator commands during a live update?

No. Preactivation actuator-invariant checks address whether the candidate state may be used; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate the sequence of effective actuator writes across a handoff. The broader goal still requires no duplicated or skipped actuator commands during an uninterrupted update.
Does it establish that every 1-ms deadline is met?

No. Bounding migration work is relevant to timing, but the proposal supplies neither a specific bound nor timing measurements. It must be integrated so that the controller continues to meet every 1 ms control deadline throughout an uninterrupted update; that remains an outcome to establish.
And does retaining the previous committed pair establish recovery after any update-time reset?

Not alone. Retention provides a proposed compatible choice if a candidate is rejected, but recovery after any update-time reset also depends on what boot can identify and use following an interruption. This proposal does not specify reset points, boot selection, or a recovery test.
How should I word the failure path without implying that the candidate firmware was activated?

Say: “If a migrated shadow candidate fails an actuator-invariant check, reject it before activation and retain the previous committed firmware-state pair.” That makes it clear the failed candidate does not become the effective pair.
What should I avoid claiming about the bound and the invariant checks?

Avoid assigning an unstated numerical migration limit, naming actuator invariants that have not been defined, or reporting that a candidate passed or failed any check. Here, bounded execution, schema typing, and preactivation rejection describe the proposed design, not completed measurements.
Can you put the whole proposal in one concise sentence?
“Proposal: Run bounded, schema-typed state migrations in shadow slots; if an actuator invariant fails, reject the candidate before activation and retain the previous committed firmware-state pair.”
Which v2→v3 actuator-state invariants must shadow migration check to prevent an unsafe command jump at activation?

The version labels alone do not specify the actuator-state fields, the allowed command changes, or what counts as an unsafe jump. The question is therefore still open at the level of particular invariants. A useful way to define them is to ask what must remain true across activation: the migrated state must be interpretable by v3 firmware, and the first command made effective using that state must be acceptable relative to the actuator state and command sequence immediately before activation. The acceptable relationship needs an actuator-specific definition; it cannot be inferred from “v2→v3.”
Are schema compatibility and command continuity the same invariant?

No. Schema compatibility asks whether v3 firmware can correctly use the migrated state. Command continuity asks whether activating that pair could produce an unsafe change in effective actuator output. A state could have the expected v3 form without establishing that its first effective command is acceptable. Shadow migration needs the applicable checks before activation rather than assuming a schema match answers the actuator question.
Can we simply require the first v3 command to equal the last v2 command?

That would be a particular invariant, and the information here does not establish that it is necessary or sufficient. An allowed activation might involve a change in command; conversely, equal command values might not by themselves establish safe actuator behavior. The design needs to define what constitutes an unsafe jump for this controller before choosing an equality rule or a permitted range.
Should we specify a maximum permitted jump, then?

Only if the actuator requirements provide a justified limit. No command units, permitted difference, or threshold are given, so I cannot supply a numerical maximum. The important question for the migration check is whether it can establish, before activation, that the command transition satisfies the applicable safety criterion.
Does checking the converted state itself tell us what command will be issued at activation?

Not automatically. A state check and an effective-command check answer different questions. To prevent the unsafe jump described in your question, the chosen invariants would need to connect the migrated actuator state to the command that can become effective at activation. Exactly how that connection is evaluated depends on the firmware and actuator semantics, which are not specified here.
What should we compare the candidate state against?

The comparison has to be anchored in the effective actuator context before activation, not merely in another candidate representation. Conceptually, you would want to know whether moving from the currently effective state and command to the candidate’s initial effective behavior satisfies the defined actuator invariants. That does not prescribe which fields are compared or how a command is calculated.
Could the migration pass if every individual v3 state field is within its allowed range?

Individual field checks may be relevant, but they would not necessarily establish a safe transition. The unsafe-jump concern is relational: what happens when the effective choice changes from the preactivation context to the v3 context. Without a specified invariant relating those contexts, valid-looking individual fields are not enough to answer the question.
Does the question require checking actuator-command sequences too?

Sequence consistency remains a separate live-update obligation: intended actuator commands must not be duplicated or skipped. For this question, the immediate focus is whether migrated actuator state can cause an unsafe command jump at activation. Checking the state transition cannot replace checking the effective command sequence, and sequence uniqueness alone cannot show that a command change is safe.
If the first v3 command has a new sequence number, does that make the jump safe?

No. A sequence number can help distinguish commits, but it does not determine whether the command value or actuator behavior is safe relative to the preactivation state. Conversely, a command that meets a safety criterion could still violate the no-duplicate-or-skip requirement if committed under the wrong sequence. Both questions need their own criteria.
Should the shadow migration reject a candidate if it cannot establish the actuator invariant?

Under the proposed preactivation-check approach, a candidate should not be activated on the assumption that an unverified invariant holds. The stated proposal is to reject actuator-invariant failures before activation and retain the previous committed firmware-state pair. The precise treatment of a check that cannot be completed has not been specified, so it would need an explicit rule rather than being silently treated as a pass.
Does “before activation” mean we can check after the first v3 command and roll back if it looks wrong?

No. That would not prevent an unsafe command jump at activation. The question asks which invariants shadow migration must check so the candidate can be assessed before it becomes effective. Observing an unsafe first command and then rolling back would occur after the event the check is meant to prevent.
Can a shadow slot contain a fully converted v3 state while the previous pair stays effective?

That is the conceptual separation the shadow-slot proposal relies on: candidate migration and checking need not make the candidate the effective firmware-state pair. The question is what actuator-state properties of that candidate must be established before activation. It does not say that a particular v2→v3 candidate has already been converted or validated.
Is the previous committed pair what we retain if an actuator invariant fails?

That is the proposed rejection behavior: an actuator-invariant failure prevents activation of the shadow candidate, leaving the previous committed firmware-state pair effective. It avoids treating a partially accepted migration as an acceptable way to handle a failed preactivation check.
Can you give me a checklist without pretending we know the actuator-specific limits?

At the conceptual level, define the v2→v3 state correspondence; identify which migrated actuator-state properties v3 firmware needs for its first effective command; define what makes the transition from the preactivation command context to that command acceptable; and specify how the check establishes those properties before activation. Also keep the independent no-duplicate-or-skip sequence check in view. This is a checklist of questions to resolve, not a list of known actuator fields, thresholds, or already verified invariants.
Would a check that the two schemas match be enough to answer every item on that checklist?

No. Matching schemas addresses whether the chosen state has a suitable form for its firmware. It does not define how far an actuator command may change at activation or whether the transition respects the controller’s actuator-state constraints. Those conditions must be specified independently where the schema does not encode them.
Should we assume every difference between the preactivation and postactivation commands is unsafe?

That assumption is not supplied. “Unsafe command jump” implies a distinction between acceptable and unacceptable transitions, but the boundary between them has not been defined. Treat that distinction as something the actuator-state invariants must make explicit rather than inventing either an all-changes-forbidden rule or a numerical tolerance.
What is the shortest faithful answer to the original question?

The specific v2→v3 actuator-state invariants cannot be named from the information given. Define checks that establish, before shadow-state activation, both a state usable by v3 firmware and an acceptable transition to its first effective actuator command; specify the actuator-dependent meaning of “unsafe jump” rather than assuming a threshold or that schema matching alone is sufficient.

I have a hypothesis for the v2→v3 shadow migration: preserve actuator mode and the next-command sequence, limit torque discontinuity to ≤0.2 N·m, and limit slew to ≤1 N·m/ms. Together, these checks should reject unsafe migrations. Is that a precise statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It names two continuity checks—actuator mode and next-command sequence—and two numerical limits: torque discontinuity of no more than 0.2 N·m and slew of no more than 1 N·m/ms. The proposed outcome is that these checks reject unsafe v2→v3 migrations. That outcome still needs to be established; stating the checks does not show that they catch every unsafe transition.
What does preserving actuator mode mean at activation?

It means the migration must not change the effective actuator mode merely as a consequence of translating v2 state into v3 state. A concrete check would need an unambiguous correspondence between the mode before migration and the mode represented in the candidate state. The hypothesis does not name any modes or define their encoding.
Does that prohibit the controller from ever changing actuator mode?

No. This is an invariant for the v2→v3 migration and its activation, not a general prohibition on authorized mode changes during ordinary operation. The proposed check is meant to prevent the migration itself from introducing an unintended mode change.
Why include the next-command sequence as well as actuator mode?

They protect different aspects of continuity. Preserving mode concerns how the actuator is configured across the state change. Preserving the next-command sequence concerns which intended command comes next, so migration does not silently move the command position forward or backward. Matching the mode alone would not establish sequence continuity.
Does preserving the next-command sequence mean the next actuator command must have the same torque value as the last one?

No. The next-command sequence identifies the position in the intended command order; it does not determine the command’s torque value. The ≤0.2 N·m discontinuity and ≤1 N·m/ms slew limits address torque behavior separately.
Is the sequence check the same as proving there will be no duplicate or skipped actuator writes?

Not by itself. Preserving the next-command sequence through the migrated state is a proposed safeguard, but the effective actuator-commit path must also issue commands without duplication or omission. A correctly migrated sequence value would not alone prove that the handoff commits each intended command exactly once.
How should I read the ≤0.2 N·m limit?

Under the hypothesis, the torque discontinuity associated with activation must be no greater than 0.2 N·m. The inequality includes a discontinuity of exactly 0.2 N·m; a greater discontinuity would fail that proposed check. The hypothesis does not yet define precisely which preactivation and postactivation torque quantities are compared.
Can I call 0.2 N·m the maximum allowed torque slew?

No. Torque discontinuity has units of N·m, while slew has units of N·m/ms. The hypothesis sets separate limits: ≤0.2 N·m for discontinuity and ≤1 N·m/ms for slew. They should not be substituted for one another.
What does the slew limit constrain that the discontinuity limit does not?

It constrains the rate at which torque changes, expressed in N·m per millisecond, rather than just the size of a discontinuity at activation. A candidate needs to satisfy both proposed conditions. The hypothesis does not specify the exact interval or command samples used to evaluate slew, so that definition would need to be made explicit before applying the check.
Since the control deadline is 1 ms, can I replace the slew limit with a 1 N·m jump limit?

No. Multiplying 1 N·m/ms by 1 ms gives 1 N·m as arithmetic, but that does not replace the separate ≤0.2 N·m discontinuity limit or define how slew is measured. The 1-ms control deadline also does not, on its own, specify the interval over which the migration’s torque slew must be checked.
Could a candidate pass the discontinuity check but still fail the slew check?

Conceptually, yes: the two checks assess different properties. A torque transition can be within the proposed discontinuity bound without that fact alone establishing compliance with the rate bound. Both need their own defined evaluation rather than inferring one from the other.
And could it pass the torque limits but still need rejection?
Under the hypothesis, yes, if it fails to preserve actuator mode or the next-command sequence. Meeting the numerical torque limits would not excuse a change to either of those continuity properties.
Should a failed check be found before the shadow state is activated?

Yes. The point of checking the shadow migration is to reject an unsafe candidate before it becomes the effective firmware-state pair. Detecting a mode, sequence, discontinuity, or slew violation only after issuing a command would not prevent the activation-time problem the hypothesis addresses.
Does rejection mean changing the effective state and then rolling it back?

No. The proposed rejection path keeps a candidate that fails an applicable invariant from being activated. Rolling back after an unsafe command jump would not make the jump safe. The hypothesis does not specify the internal representation of rejected shadow state.
What exactly needs definition before these checks could be applied?

The design would need to define the v2-to-v3 correspondence for actuator mode and next-command sequence, which torque values are compared for the activation discontinuity, and how torque slew is evaluated. Those definitions must preserve the stated limits of ≤0.2 N·m and ≤1 N·m/ms. No particular fields, sampling procedure, or conversion formula are supplied in the hypothesis.
Can schema typing alone establish that these four checks pass?

No. A state can have the expected v3 schema without preserving its actuator mode or next-command sequence, and without meeting the two torque limits. Schema typing makes the candidate interpretable for checking; it does not replace the actuator-state invariants.
If all four checks pass, may I state that the migration is proven safe?

Not yet. The hypothesis is that these checks reject unsafe v2→v3 migrations. Passing them would establish compliance with the checks as defined and applied, but the information here does not establish that they cover every possible actuator hazard or that a particular migration has passed. Keep the safety conclusion at the level of a hypothesis until it is supported.
Would a missed 1-ms control deadline count as a failure of the torque-slew invariant?

It would be a failure of the separate real-time deadline requirement, not a measurement of torque slew. An uninterrupted update must meet every 1-ms deadline as well as preserve actuator consistency. The proposed migration invariants do not make a late control cycle acceptable.
Does this hypothesis say anything about recovery after a reset during migration?

No. It proposes preactivation checks for rejecting unsafe v2→v3 shadow migrations. Recovering a compatible firmware-state pair after an update-time reset is a separate requirement; these four invariants do not, by themselves, specify boot recovery behavior.
Can you state the hypothesis compactly without implying that the numerical limits have already been measured?

“Hypothesis: Checking that a v2→v3 shadow migration preserves actuator mode and next-command sequence, limits torque discontinuity to ≤0.2 N·m, and limits slew to ≤1 N·m/ms will reject unsafe candidates before activation.” The limits are proposed checks, not reported measurements.

I want a plan for the v2→v3 shadow migration: define migration contracts, generate boundary and corrupt-state fixtures, then test atomic rejection and first-command actuator continuity. How should I organize it?

Organize it in that order. First specify what a valid v2→v3 migration must preserve and what makes a candidate unacceptable. Then prepare fixtures that exercise the edges of those contracts and fixtures containing corrupt state. Finally, run the migration and activation checks against those fixtures, observing whether unacceptable candidates are rejected atomically and whether an accepted candidate’s first effective actuator command is continuous with the preactivation context. This is a plan, not a report of test outcomes.
What belongs in a migration contract here?

The contract should state the expected relationship between the v2 input state and the candidate v3 state, including the actuator-state conditions that must hold before activation. It should also make clear which conditions cause rejection. The plan does not provide particular state fields or conversion formulas, so those details must be defined rather than assumed.
Is a contract just a declaration that the v3 state has the right schema?

No. Having a v3-shaped result is only part of the question. The contract also needs to express the conditions relevant to activating that result without an unacceptable actuator transition. Otherwise, a candidate could be structurally interpretable yet still fail the first-command continuity check the plan calls for.
Should the contracts distinguish the migration result from its activation?

Yes. Producing candidate v3 state and making a firmware-state pair effective are different events. A contract should permit the candidate to be assessed before activation, so an unacceptable result can be rejected without first exposing it as effective state.
Does the plan say exactly which actuator invariants the contract must encode?

It calls for defining v2→v3 migration contracts but does not itself enumerate the final checks or their implementation. The contract must be specific enough to assess the actuator behavior at activation; it would be premature to invent fields, values, or criteria beyond those established for the design.
What do you mean by boundary fixtures?

They are test inputs chosen around the limits or transitions defined in the migration contracts. They help examine whether a candidate at a contract boundary is treated differently from one outside it when that distinction matters. Which fixtures to generate depends on the contracts; the plan supplies no particular values or number of cases.
Are boundary fixtures necessarily invalid?

No. A boundary can include a case that satisfies a contract and a nearby case that does not. The purpose is to make the acceptance and rejection behavior at the defined edge observable, not to assume every boundary fixture must fail.
Could we generate the boundary cases first and decide the contract afterward?

The stated sequence is to define the contracts first, then generate fixtures against them. That gives the boundary cases a clear meaning and lets the tests judge outcomes against specified expectations rather than adjusting the rules to match what happens.
How are corrupt-state fixtures different from boundary fixtures?

A boundary fixture probes a defined edge of an otherwise specified migration condition. A corrupt-state fixture presents state that is damaged or unsuitable for the expected input or candidate. The categories may exercise different reasons for rejection, but the plan does not specify any particular corruption pattern or say every boundary case is corrupt.
Should I assume corruption means a bad CRC?

No. The plan says “corrupt-state fixtures” without limiting corruption to a CRC failure. A concrete test suite would need to define its fixtures and expected outcomes. Do not substitute one particular detection mechanism for the broader fixture category in the plan.
What is the atomic-rejection test meant to observe?

It should determine whether a candidate that must be rejected leaves the effective firmware-state choice unchanged rather than partly activating the migration. The key observation is the effective outcome: rejection must not expose a partial v3 state or an incompatible firmware-state combination. Inspecting only a rejection message would not establish that property.
If migration writes some data to a shadow slot and then rejects the candidate, is that automatically an atomic-rejection failure?

No. Candidate work can occur in a shadow slot without becoming effective. Atomic rejection concerns whether the rejected candidate, or any partial result of it, changes the effective firmware-state pair. The plan does not require that every trace of rejected preparation be erased immediately.
Would a failed contract check after activation count as rejection?

It would not demonstrate the planned preactivation atomic rejection. If an unacceptable candidate first becomes effective, an eventual rejection or rollback cannot erase that exposure. The test needs to distinguish a candidate rejected before activation from a problem detected only afterward.
What should we measure for first-command actuator continuity?

Compare the first effective actuator command after activation with the preactivation actuator context under the continuity conditions specified in the contract. The question is whether activation introduces an unacceptable command transition. The plan does not state an actuator value, a permitted change, or a measurement method, so those must not be supplied as though already decided here.
Is observing the candidate’s calculated first command sufficient?

Not on its own. A calculated command is not necessarily the command that becomes effective at the actuator. For the planned continuity test, distinguish the candidate’s prospective output from the first command actually committed after activation.
Could the first postactivation command have a different value and still pass?

That depends on the contract’s continuity criterion. The plan asks for first-command actuator continuity, not unconditional equality of command values. It should determine whether the observed transition meets the defined condition rather than assume every change is forbidden or every change is acceptable.
If the first command is continuous, does that prove the entire command sequence has no duplicates or skips?

No. First-command continuity focuses on the activation transition. The broader live-update goal also requires avoiding duplicated and skipped actuator commands throughout an uninterrupted update. One favorable first-command observation would not establish every later per-sequence outcome.
Should first-command continuity be checked for a rejected fixture too?

For a rejected candidate, the central check is that it never activates, so there should be no first effective command from that candidate to assess. You can still observe that the effective actuator path remains consistent during rejection, but do not describe a rejected candidate as having a postactivation first command.
How do the two test objectives relate when a fixture is accepted?

An accepted candidate gives you an activation whose first effective command can be checked for continuity. For a fixture that the contract requires to reject, the primary question is whether rejection is atomic. The same contract supplies the basis for deciding which outcome is expected; the plan does not presume that every fixture has the same expected result.
Would simply checking that the v3 firmware starts establish either objective?

No. Starting firmware does not establish that a rejected migration left the effective choice unchanged, nor does it show that the first effective actuator command made an acceptable transition. The planned observations must address atomic rejection and command continuity directly.
Does this plan specify resets at every flash-write boundary?

No. It specifies migration contracts, boundary and corrupt-state fixtures, and tests of atomic rejection and first-command continuity. It does not provide a reset-injection schedule or claim complete flash-write-boundary coverage.
Does it verify that control meets every 1-ms deadline during conversion?

Not by itself. The controller still has that uninterrupted-update requirement, but this plan’s explicit test objectives are atomic rejection and first-command actuator continuity. Do not treat the presence of bounded migration or a successful continuity check as a deadline measurement.
Can I call the migration safe as soon as its contracts have been written?

No. Defining contracts makes expected behavior explicit. Boundary and corrupt-state fixtures then exercise those expectations, and the tests examine the effective rejection and first-command outcomes. Writing the contract is a prerequisite for meaningful checks, not evidence that the migration meets it.
What would be a clear failure of the atomic-rejection objective?

If a fixture the contract requires to reject causes any part of the candidate migration to become effective, or leaves an incompatible firmware-state choice effective, that would fail the atomic-rejection check. That is a criterion for evaluating a future observation, not a prediction that the test will find it.
And what would fail the first-command continuity objective?

For an accepted and activated candidate, a first effective actuator command that violates the contract’s defined transition condition would fail that check. The plan does not give the condition’s numerical value, so the failure should be judged against the contract rather than an invented threshold.
How can I phrase the plan concisely while keeping the ordering and both objectives?

“Define the v2→v3 migration contracts; generate boundary and corrupt-state fixtures against them; then test that unacceptable candidates are rejected atomically and that the first effective actuator command after an accepted activation satisfies the specified continuity conditions.”

I want to implement MigrationContract-v3 so it checks actuator mode, the next-command sequence, a 0.2-N·m torque-jump limit, and a 1-N·m/ms slew limit before shadow-slot commit. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as implementing a precommit check for the shadow-state candidate. MigrationContract-v3 will check mode and next-command sequence continuity, a torque jump of no more than 0.2 N·m, and slew of no more than 1 N·m/ms before the shadow slot is committed. That states what the contract is to check, not that it has been implemented or that a candidate has passed.
Does “before shadow-slot commit” mean I can run the checks after the candidate becomes effective, as long as I can roll back?

No. The ordering is part of the activity: perform the checks before committing the shadow slot. Checking after the candidate becomes effective would not prevent an unacceptable activation-time actuator transition.
What is the role of the shadow slot here?

It holds candidate migrated state separately from the effective firmware-state choice while the checks are applied. That lets the contract assess the candidate before a commit. The activity does not specify the slot’s physical layout or say how its contents are written.
Are shadow-slot commit and activation necessarily the same operation?

That is not specified here. The precise requirement in this activity is that MigrationContract-v3 checks the candidate before shadow-slot commit. Do not assume a particular relationship between the commit operation and the later effective handoff unless the design defines it.
Should the mode check just establish that the candidate contains a mode field?

That would be too weak for a continuity check. The contract needs to assess the candidate’s actuator mode in relation to the mode it is supposed to preserve across the v2→v3 migration. The activity does not name any modes or specify how they are encoded.
Does checking mode forbid all future changes of actuator mode?
No. The check concerns what this migration does to actuator state before its shadow slot is committed. It does not set a general rule for every mode change during ordinary controller operation.
What should “next-command sequence” mean in the contract?

It is the sequence position the migrated state presents as the next intended actuator command. Checking it helps detect a migration that would move that position unexpectedly across the schema change. The activity does not give a sequence value or define a particular encoding.
If the next sequence is preserved, can I infer that actuator writes will never be duplicated or skipped?

No. Preserving the sequence in migrated state is one precommit condition. The effective actuator-commit path must still handle commands correctly through the handoff. A correct state value alone does not prove that each intended sequence receives exactly one effective write.
How should I interpret the 0.2-N·m torque-jump check?

Treat 0.2 N·m as the proposed upper bound on the torque discontinuity being checked before commit. A jump of exactly 0.2 N·m is within a ≤0.2 N·m limit; a larger one is not. The activity does not define the precise torque quantities used on either side of that comparison.
Could I express that limit in N·m/ms instead?
No. A torque jump is a difference measured in N·m. The separate slew check is a rate measured in N·m/ms. Changing the units would conflate the two checks.
What does the 1-N·m/ms slew check add?

It checks how rapidly torque changes, with a proposed limit of ≤1 N·m/ms. That is distinct from checking the size of the activation jump against 0.2 N·m. The contract will need a defined way to evaluate slew, but this activity does not supply the interval or samples used.
If a candidate satisfies the torque-jump limit, can the slew check be skipped?

No. The activity calls for both checks. Passing the jump check does not, by itself, establish compliance with the rate limit, just as passing slew does not establish that the activation discontinuity is within 0.2 N·m.
Should I describe those values as measurements already obtained from a migration?
No. They are limits that MigrationContract-v3 is to check. This activity provides no observed torque jump, observed slew, or contract-check result for a particular migration.
What if the candidate passes both numerical checks but changes actuator mode?

Then it has not satisfied all the specified checks. The torque limits do not substitute for preserving mode. The same applies if its next-command sequence is wrong: all four conditions need to be evaluated before the shadow-slot commit.
Can I describe the contract as checking schema compatibility in general?

The name MigrationContract-v3 and the shadow-slot context identify a v3 migration contract, but the checks specified in this activity are mode, next-command sequence, the 0.2-N·m torque jump, and the 1-N·m/ms slew. Do not imply that this list, by itself, defines every possible schema-compatibility check.
What should happen if one of these checks fails?

A failed precommit check should not be treated as permission to commit that shadow candidate. The point of implementing the checks before commit is to keep an unacceptable candidate from becoming the committed migration result. The activity does not report a failure or specify the internal handling of a rejected shadow slot.
Could I claim that the contract now rejects every unsafe v2→v3 migration?

No. This is an implementation activity, not evidence of completed coverage. The four checks are specified, but whether they correctly detect every unsafe migration—or whether a particular implementation applies them correctly—remains to be evaluated.
Does this implementation activity also test first-command continuity?

It puts precommit conditions in place that are relevant to first-command continuity, particularly sequence, torque jump, and slew.
